stories.actor: A man captured with his mother; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother were taken captive and he never stopped watching over her.
stories.turn: His remark was offhand, not formal testimony, though a son cannot normally testify for his mother.
stories.outcome: Rabbi permitted the mother to marry into the priesthood on the basis of his remark.
stories.summary: A man, speaking offhandedly, said that he and his mother had been captured by gentiles and that his thoughts were always on her whether drawing water or gathering wood. The case came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who relied on this incidental remark and allowed her to marry a priest.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav
stories.event: He swore that his wife's hand never left his during the gentile occupation of Jerusalem.
stories.turn: The Sages rejected his testimony because a man cannot testify about himself, so his wife was forbidden to him.
stories.outcome: He did not divorce her but gave her a separate house in his courtyard and avoided being alone with her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav, a priest, swore that his wife had never left his side while gentiles occupied Jerusalem. The Sages refused his testimony, since one cannot testify about oneself, and she was forbidden to him. He kept her in a house in his courtyard, arranging that she went in and out only with her sons so they were never alone together.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rabbi Meyasha's family; Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership was disputed between the depositor and the heirs.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the claimant gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who died without saying whose they were. The parties went to Rabbi Ami, who ruled for the depositor because he knew Rabbi Meyasha could not afford such gems and the claimant described them.

stories.actor: A depositor and Hasa's heirs; Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman gave it to the depositor because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Rav Nahman ruled that it belonged to the depositor, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant provided an identifying mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs; Rabbi Abba
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership of the silk was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: Someone deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving word about it. Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant could identify it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, Rabbi Afes and Levi
stories.event: Rabbi Hanina refused to head the yeshiva ahead of the older Rabbi Afes and sat outside, joined by Levi.
stories.turn: Rabbi Afes died and Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, leaving Levi without a study partner.
stories.outcome: Levi went to Babylonia, and Rav, hearing of a limping scholar teaching in Neharde'a, deduced what had happened.
stories.summary: Although appointed head of the yeshiva, Rabbi Hanina bar Hama deferred to Rabbi Afes, who was older, and sat outside; Levi sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took his place, and Levi, with no one to study with, left for Babylonia. When Rav was told a great limping man had come to Neharde'a and was teaching, he concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Rabbi Hanina had taken over.

stories.actor: A man, a woman washing her feet; Rava
stories.event: A man grabbed coins from someone and threw them to a woman, declaring her betrothed.
stories.turn: The coins were stolen.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal ineffective, since the owner is not presumed to have despaired of stolen money.
stories.summary: While a woman was washing her feet, a man snatched some dinars from another person, threw them to her and said she was betrothed to him. Rava ruled that the coins were still the owner's, so the betrothal was void.

stories.actor: A sharecropper; Rava
stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: The owner had not permitted him to take them.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the onions were stolen, so the betrothal failed.
stories.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions taken from his employer's field. Rava asked who had given him the onions and ruled them stolen property, so the woman was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A brewer and the beer's owner; Rava
stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with beer sediment belonging to his client.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he didn't use the better sediment.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that this remark did not count as consent outside teruma, so the betrothal failed.
stories.summary: A brewer used sediment from someone else's date beer to betroth a woman. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the better sediment. Rava ruled that 'go take the better ones' counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.

stories.actor: Homa, Abaye's widow; Rava; Rava's wife
stories.event: Homa came to Rava's court to claim support and wine from Abaye's estate.
stories.turn: As she gestured, her arm was exposed and her beauty dazzled Rava, who went home aroused.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife learned who had been in court and drove Homa out of Mehoza with a chest lock, accusing her of killing three husbands.
stories.summary: Abaye's widow Homa asked Rava for support and then for wine; Rava doubted Abaye drank wine, but she insisted he gave her large cups and gestured, exposing her arm, which seemed to light up the court. Rava went home and asked his wife for relations. She asked who had been in court, and on hearing it was Homa, she chased Homa out of the city, striking her and saying she had already killed three husbands and would not kill a fourth.

stories.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava; Rav Nehemya
stories.event: She asked Rav Nehemya to allot her sustenance and wine.
stories.turn: Rav Nehemya considered the local custom.
stories.outcome: He granted wine because Mehoza residents drink wine.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava came to Rav Nehemya for support and then for wine. He granted both, noting that the people of Mehoza are accustomed to drinking wine.

stories.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya; Rav Yosef
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef for sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef questioned why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered that it was for appearing before him and his colleagues with dignity.
stories.summary: A widow came to Rav Yosef, who granted her food and wine. When she also asked for silk garments, he asked why, and she replied that they were for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so she would not be shamed before them.

stories.actor: A woman litigant; Rav Beivai bar Abaye; Rav Pappi
stories.event: A woman required to take an oath demanded a document of rights written in advance before swearing in town.
stories.turn: Rav Beivai ordered the document written, and Rav Pappi mocked him for the ruling.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappi rebuked Rav Beivai, calling his statement unfortunate.
stories.summary: A woman was obliged to swear an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court, and her opponent asked that she swear in town, hoping shame would make her confess. She agreed only if the court first wrote her a document of rights, and Rav Beivai ordered it written. Rav Pappi scoffed that he spoke unfortunate words because he came from an unfortunate family.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Yehuda bar Mareimar and Abba of Sura
stories.event: Rav Pappa pressed a reluctant Yehuda bar Mareimar to join him at the writing of his son's marriage contract.
stories.turn: Yehuda sat silently, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, wrote all his property into the dowry.
stories.outcome: Yehuda said he disapproved, but told Abba not to retract and become a man who goes back on his word.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa went to the family of Abba of Sura to write the marriage contract for his son, and Yehuda bar Mareimar escorted him but did not want to go in, fearing his presence would pressure the bride's father. Rav Pappa forced him to enter; he sat in silence, and Abba of Sura, assuming he was displeased, signed away everything he owned as dowry. Yehuda said he had not wanted even that, and when Abba offered to retract, Yehuda told him not to make himself someone who goes back on his word.

stories.actor: A divorcee; Shmuel; Rav Dimi bar Yosef
stories.event: A divorcee who did not want to nurse her son came before Shmuel, who sent Rav Dimi to test whether the baby recognized her.
stories.turn: Carried past a row of women, the baby looked joyfully at her while she averted her eyes.
stories.outcome: Rav Dimi told her to look up and take her son.
stories.summary: A divorced woman came before Shmuel, unwilling to nurse her baby. Rav Dimi bar Yosef placed her among a row of women and carried the child past them; the baby gazed happily at her while she looked away. He told her to lift her eyes and take her son, since he clearly knew her.

stories.actor: A depositor and Hasa's heirs; Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the depositor because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Rav Nahman ruled that it belonged to the depositor, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant provided an identifying mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs; Rabbi Abba
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership of the silk was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the depositor.
stories.summary: Someone deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving word about it. Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant could identify it.

stories.actor: A dying man and Toviya; Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to Toviya and died.
stories.turn: A Toviya came to claim it, raising the question of whether he was the intended one.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and receives the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After his death a man named Toviya arrived to claim it, and Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

stories.actor: A depositor and Hasa's heirs; Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the depositor because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a mark.
stories.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Rav Nahman ruled that it belonged to the depositor, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant provided an identifying mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs; Rabbi Abba
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Ownership of the silk was disputed.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the depositor.
stories.summary: Someone deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving word about it. Rabbi Abba ruled the silk belonged to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant could identify it.

stories.actor: A dying man and Toviya; Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to Toviya and died.
stories.turn: A Toviya came to claim it, raising the question of whether he was the intended one.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and receives the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After his death a man named Toviya arrived to claim it, and Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

stories.actor: Ze'eiri and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Ze'eiri kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan's offer of his daughter in marriage.
stories.turn: When Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a puddle, Rabbi Yohanan confronted him: our Torah is fit but our daughters are not?
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan argued that lineage in Babylonia was no purer, though the Gemara notes he missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching.
stories.summary: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian, avoided Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter. One day Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan on his shoulders across a puddle, and Rabbi Yohanan asked why he honored their Torah but would not marry their daughters. He argued that families of flawed lineage had remained in Babylonia too.

stories.actor: Ulla and Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Visiting Pumbedita, Ulla saw that Rav Yehuda's grown son was unmarried and asked why.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda feared flawed lineage, and Ulla answered that no one can be sure of his own ancestry.
stories.outcome: Ulla advised him to pick a family by its silence, the way people in Eretz Yisrael judge which quarreler is of finer lineage.
stories.summary: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda and asked why his grown son Rav Yitzhak had not been married off. Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a wife of sound lineage; Ulla replied that none of them really knew their own descent, citing verses about ravished women and depraved ancestors. When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla told him to look for the family that falls silent first in a quarrel.

stories.actor: A seller of glass beads and a woman; Rav Hama
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' is meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man selling glass beads was asked by a woman for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she replied 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this mocking reply meant nothing, so there was no betrothal.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman; Rav Hama
stories.event: A woman in a tavern asked a man for a cup of wine, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give to drink, give it to me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled her answer meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup of wine, and he asked if she would be betrothed with it. She replied 'Pour, pour me a drink,' and Rav Hama ruled this was no agreement, so she was not betrothed.

stories.actor: A man picking dates and a woman; Rav Zevid
stories.event: A woman asked a man knocking down dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed by them.
stories.turn: She answered 'Throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled the answer meaningless and she was not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman asked a man in a date palm to throw her two dates. He asked whether she would then be betrothed to him, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that such a reply is nothing, so there was no betrothal.

stories.actor: Two pious men, perhaps Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas
stories.event: One fed the waiter before the meal and the other after.
stories.turn: Elijah's regard differed between them.
stories.outcome: Elijah spoke with the one who fed the waiter first, but not with the other.
stories.summary: Two pious men, said to be Rav Hisda's sons Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, differed in when they fed the waiter: one before the meal, one after. Elijah the prophet spoke with the one who fed him first and did not speak with the other.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's butler
stories.event: Seeing Mar Zutra grow pale with craving, Rav Ashi put some of the king's food into his mouth.
stories.turn: The butler accused him of spoiling the king's meal, and Rav Ashi claimed the meat was defective.
stories.outcome: On his pointing, leprosy was found in the meat; he told the Sages he had seen a leprous spirit over it.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as the chief butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra blanch with craving and put some in his mouth with his finger; when accused of spoiling the king's meal, he said the meat was unfit. Nothing was found until he pointed to a spot, where leprosy turned up, and he explained to the Sages that he had seen a spirit of leprosy hovering over it.

stories.actor: A Roman and a woman
stories.event: A Roman whose proposal was refused ate pomegranates in front of the woman until her craving made her ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He ate pomegranates before her again, had her spit out the saliva, and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He peeled and ate pomegranates in front of her without sharing, and she swallowed her saliva until she became ill. When he asked whether she would marry him if he cured her, she said yes; he ate pomegranates again and told her to spit, and after something like a green leaf came out she recovered.

stories.actor: A steward of orphans; Abaye
stories.event: A deceased man had used a field as a boundary marker for another's land, then contested it, and his steward pursued the claim before Abaye.
stories.turn: Abaye ruled the claim lost, but the steward argued step by step what the father would have claimed.
stories.outcome: Abaye accepted his arguments and praised him as the kind of steward one should appoint for orphans.
stories.summary: A man had cited a field as a boundary marker attributing it to someone else, later contested it, and died, leaving a steward over his orphans. Abaye ruled that the claim was forfeited, but the steward argued that the father would have said he meant only one furrow, and then that he had bought that furrow back, and Abaye accepted both arguments. Abaye remarked that anyone appointing a steward should choose someone like this, who knows how to argue for orphans.

stories.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin; Rabbi Ami
stories.event: They bought a maidservant for copper coins they did not have, leaving a piece of silver as collateral.
stories.turn: Her price rose and the sellers wanted to cancel.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled no acquisition had taken place, since neither coins nor collateral transfer ownership.
stories.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons bought a maidservant for copper perutot but, lacking the cash, left a piece of silver as security. When her value went up, the sellers sought to back out, and Rabbi Ami ruled that neither the unpaid coins nor the collateral had completed the sale.

stories.actor: Rav Amram the Pious
stories.event: Redeemed captive women lodged in Rav Amram's attic, and one's beauty drove him to lift a heavy ladder and climb toward them.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and shouted 'Fire in Amram's house!'
stories.outcome: He told the embarrassed Sages it was better to be shamed now than in the next world, and forced his evil inclination out of him as a pillar of fire.
stories.summary: Captive women brought to Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's upper room with the ladder removed. When one passed the opening, her beauty overcame him; he lifted a ladder ten men could not carry and began to climb. Halfway he stopped himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!'; when the Sages complained he had shamed them, he said shame in this world was better than in the next, then made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire.

stories.actor: Rabbi Meir
stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan appear as a woman across a river and began crossing a rope bridge to her.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said that only heaven's warning about Rabbi Meir kept him from ruining him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river, and with no ferry he started across a rope bridge. Halfway, Satan let go and told him that only the heavenly proclamation to beware of Rabbi Meir and his Torah had saved him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva
stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan appear as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva kept him from ruining him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and he began to climb. Halfway, Satan left him and said that only heaven's warning to beware of Rabbi Akiva had protected him.

stories.actor: Peleimu
stories.event: Peleimu, who daily mocked Satan, was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a pauper.
stories.turn: The pauper demanded to come in and sit at the table, then behaved repulsively.
stories.outcome: The story is cut off as Peleimu begins to rebuke him.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say every day 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man; Peleimu gave him bread, then brought him in and seated him at the table at his insistence. Covered in boils, the guest behaved disgustingly, and Peleimu began to speak to him as the window ends.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel
stories.event: Funeral costs had become so heavy that families abandoned their dead.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen garments.
stories.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and burial in simple garments became the custom.
stories.summary: Burials had grown so lavish that the expense was harder on families than the death itself, and some fled leaving the dead unburied. Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried in plain linen, and the whole people followed his lead.

stories.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon; the Sages
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins a day for perfumes from her late husband's estate.
stories.turn: She responded by blessing them.
stories.outcome: She wished the same for their daughters, and they answered Amen.
stories.summary: When the Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for one day's perfume, she told them to provide this way for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: Leaving Jerusalem, he saw a girl picking barley from Arabs' animal dung, who asked him for support.
stories.turn: She revealed she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose marriage contract he had signed for a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and lamented that when Israel does not do God's will it is delivered even to the animals of a lowly nation.
stories.summary: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman gathering barley from the dung of Arabs' animals; she covered herself with her hair and begged him for food. She said she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, that her family's wealth was lost, and reminded him he had signed her marriage contract. He recalled the enormous dowry, wept, and said Israel's fate depends on doing God's will.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: He saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
stories.turn: Moved by the sight, he applied a verse to her.
stories.outcome: He read the Song of Songs verse as 'feed your bodies' about her plight.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swore he had seen Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter gathering barley between horses' hooves in Akko. He recited a verse from Song of Songs about her, rereading 'your kids' as 'your bodies.'

stories.actor: A blind man, a messenger and Mar Shmuel
stories.event: Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch a late blind student, but they missed each other.
stories.turn: The messenger reported that he had seen the blind man's wife committing adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, so Shmuel sent a messenger, who went one way while the blind man came another. The messenger returned saying the man's wife had committed adultery. When the blind man asked Shmuel, he was told to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not if he didn't.

stories.actor: King Yannai, Elazar ben Po'ira and the Sages
stories.event: Celebrating a victory, Yannai feasted the Sages, and Elazar ben Po'ira claimed they secretly opposed him.
stories.turn: When Yannai wore the frontplate, the elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told him to give up the priesthood, citing a rumor about his mother that proved false.
stories.outcome: Urged by Elazar, Yannai had the Sages killed, and Torah was desolate until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.
stories.summary: After conquering sixty cities, King Yannai held a feast for the Sages, where the scoundrel Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees resented him and suggested testing them with the priestly frontplate. The elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to be content with the crown and leave the priesthood, because of a rumor that his mother had been captured; the rumor was investigated and found baseless, and the Sages were expelled in anger. Elazar then urged Yannai to destroy them, saying the Torah lay in a corner for anyone to study, and all the Sages were killed until Shimon ben Shatah restored the Torah.

stories.actor: A Jew and a gentile traveling together
stories.event: A gentile who could not keep pace with a Jew reminded him of the Temple's destruction to slow him.
stories.turn: The Jew groaned but kept walking fast, and the gentile asked why groaning had not weakened him.
stories.outcome: The Jew explained that a grief long familiar no longer breaks a person.
stories.summary: A gentile walking with a Jew could not keep up, so he mentioned the destruction of the Temple to sadden him. The Jew sighed but still outpaced him, and when the gentile asked why the sigh hadn't broken him, he said that only a new sorrow does that, not one people are used to.

stories.actor: Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu, supported by two slaves in a bathhouse, was caught when it collapsed.
stories.turn: He grabbed a pillar and climbed out.
stories.outcome: He pulled both slaves up with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, held up by two slaves, when it collapsed beneath him. He caught hold of a pillar, climbed up, and lifted both slaves to safety.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Climbing stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, Rabbi Yohanan felt the stair collapse.
stories.turn: He climbed up and lifted both of them, prompting the Sages to ask why he needed support.
stories.outcome: He replied that he was saving his strength for old age.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was going up stairs with Rav Ami and Rav Asi supporting him when a step gave way. He went up and pulled them both up with him. When the Sages asked why so strong a man needed support, he said he was saving his strength for old age.
